description: Per-translation glossary overlay for the Wheel of Heaven Translation of Ezekiel. v1.0.0 (2026-11-01, Editor pass, claude-opus-5-5, wave E2: Ezek 2, 3, 8, 11, 40, 42, 43, 44) creates the overlay. It holds five book-level conventions: direct-speech quotation marks (the Kings convention), the transliteration of rûaḥ ('ruach') where it moves the prophet or is YHWH's own rûaḥ given, with 'spirit' for the human disposition (including the 'new spirit' of 11:19) and 'side' for the compass sense, English forms of proper names (the ezekiel-woh precedent, which differs from the Kings overlays), Ketiv/Qere (Qere translated), and the MT baseline at versional cruxes, including paragraph marks and supplied words. It also holds twelve text-specific decisions: raʿaš 'rumbling' (3:12-13); the scroll 'written on the front and on the back' (2:9-3:3); nep̄eš 'life' (3:19, 21); tabnîṯ/toḵnîṯ/təḵûnâ 'pattern'/'plan'/'arrangement'; śārîm 'officials' and nāśîʾ 'prince'; the Temple-vision vocabulary tāʾ 'guardroom', ʾêlām 'vestibule' (inferred), ʾayil 'post', the units of measurement, the altar terms, and harʾēl/ʾăriʾêl 'altar hearth' (inferred); and qōḏeš for the holy chambers and garments (42:13-14; 44:19). The signed-off chapters 1, 10 and 37 predate the overlay and are not retro-edited; their divergences are listed in wave-e2-editor-report.md. Candidates for promotion to central: the rûaḥ transliteration (shared with the Kings overlays) and the quotation-mark convention.

entries.translit: wayyōʾmer ʾēlay / lēʾmōr / kōh ʾāmar ʾăḏōnāy YHWH / nəʾum ʾăḏōnāy YHWH
entries.lemma: direct speech and the Hebrew formulas that introduce and close it
entries.literal: Biblical Hebrew has no quotation marks; speech is marked by verbs of saying, by lēʾmōr 'saying', and by the messenger and oracle formulas
entries.standardEnglish: ASV: no quotation marks; NRSV and NJPS: quotation marks
entries.wohChoice: Double quotation marks for direct speech; single quotes for speech within speech (the message the prophet is told to deliver, which opens with 'Thus says the Lord YHWH', and words quoted inside a speech); double quotes again at a third level. A speech that runs across several verses opens in its first verse and closes in its last, with no reopening at verse starts. A formula that ends a verse and introduces a speech in the next ('the word of YHWH came to me, saying:') takes a colon. The oracle formula nəʾum ʾăḏōnāy YHWH ('declares the Lord YHWH') stays inside the speech it belongs to. Where the Hebrew introduces no new speaker, a speech stays open until the next narrative frame (43:7-17, closed before 'He said to me' in 43:18).
entries.rationale: Quotation marks are editorial in any English Bible; the decision concerns consistency, not meaning. The Kings books ratified this convention at the wave-A and wave-B sign-offs (double quotes, nested single quotes, multi-verse speeches opened once; see 1KI-WOH-22:19-23 for triple nesting), and the Reviewer then required the Kings chapters to apply it without exception. The signed-off Ezekiel chapters are not consistent: 10:2, 6 and 37:3, 4, 9, 11, 18 quote dialogue, but 37:5, 12-14, 16, 19 and 21-28 leave the messenger formula and the oracle that follows it unquoted. The book's commissioning narratives and its long oracles (2:3-8; 3:17-21; 11:5-12; 43:18-27; 44:6-31) contain speech within speech, which only nested marks show clearly. Ezekiel therefore adopts the Kings convention from this wave on, and the speech boundaries follow the Hebrew introductory formulas. Where the Hebrew does not mark where a speech ends (43:7-17: no new speaker is introduced before 'He said to me' in 43:18, and the direct address 'As for you, son of human' in 43:10 belongs to the speech), the speech is kept open until the next narrative frame. Chapters 1, 10 and 37 are not edited in this pass. Their alignment with this entry (chiefly ch. 37) is listed as a follow-up in the wave-E2 editor report. A stack simulation over the eight wave-E2 chapters confirms that every quotation opens and closes in balance.

entries.source: רוּחַ / רוּחַ יְהוָה / רוּחַ אֱלֹהִים / רוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה / רוּחַ (צַד)
entries.translit: rûaḥ / rûaḥ YHWH / rûaḥ ʾĕlōhîm / rûaḥ ḥăḏāšâ / rûaḥ ('side')
entries.literal: wind / breath / spirit; quarter of the compass
entries.standardEnglish: the Spirit (ASV 2:2; 3:12, 14, 24; 8:3; 11:1, 24; 43:5); the Spirit of Jehovah (ASV 11:5); a new spirit (ASV 11:19); 'a spirit' (NRSV, NJPS 2:2); side (ASV 42:16-20)
entries.wohChoice: 'ruach' (roman, without an English article unless the Hebrew has one) where rûaḥ is the agent that enters the prophet, sets him on his feet, lifts him or carries him (2:2; 3:12, 14a, 24; 8:3; 11:1, 24a; 43:5); 'the ruach of YHWH' for rûaḥ YHWH (11:5a) and 'the ruach of Elohim' for bərûaḥ ʾĕlōhîm (11:24b, no English article, as in 'visions of Elohim'); 'ruach' also where YHWH gives his own rûaḥ (37:5-6, 14; later 36:27 'my rûaḥ'). 'Spirit' (lower case) where rûaḥ is the human disposition or mind: in idioms (3:14b baḥămaṯ rûḥî 'in the heat of my spirit'; 11:5b maʿălôṯ rûḥăḵem 'the things that come up in your spirit') and where a new disposition is given, paired with the heart (11:19 'a new spirit'; later 18:31; 36:26a). 'Side' where rûaḥ is a side or quarter of a measured area (42:16-19; 42:20 ʾarbaʿ rûḥôṯ 'the four sides'). The rûaḥ of the living creatures (1:12, 20-21; 10:17) remains under central ruach-chayyot, and the four rûḥôt of 37:9 under central ruach-arba-ruchot.
entries.rationale: rûaḥ covers 'wind', 'breath' and 'spirit' (BDB; HALOT rûaḥ), and Ezekiel uses the word some fifty times in nearly every sense. Block ('The Prophet of the Spirit: The Use of rwḥ in the Book of Ezekiel', JETS 32, 1989) classifies these uses as wind, side or direction, mind or disposition, and the rûaḥ as agent of conveyance, of animation and of inspiration. At the transport sites rûaḥ is usually anarthrous with a feminine verb (wattiśśāʾēnî rûaḥ, 3:12; 43:5), and interpreters divide between a wind associated with the theophany (cf. rûaḥ səʿārâ, 1:4) and the divine spirit. NJPS has 'a spirit', NRSV 'the spirit' or 'a spirit', and the ASV 'the Spirit', whose capital decides the question in favour of the later doctrine of a personal Holy Spirit, which the Hebrew does not state. The signed-off precedent in this book transliterates exactly this use (37:1 'by the ruach of YHWH'; 37:5-6, 14), and the Kings overlays do the same for the rûaḥ YHWH that carries a prophet away (1 Kgs 18:12; 2 Kgs 2:16; entry ruach-yhwh-and-prophetic-ruach-transliteration-kings). Transliteration leaves the acknowledged ambiguity open and keeps one Hebrew word visible across the book: the rûaḥ in the wheels (1:20), the rûaḥ that lifts the prophet (3:12; 8:3; 11:1), and YHWH's own rûaḥ that he gives (36:27; 37:14). Two senses are not ambiguous and are translated: the human disposition, whether in idioms (3:14b; 11:5b) or as the 'new spirit' that YHWH gives together with a new heart (11:19; cf. 18:31, where Israel is told to make itself 'a new heart and a new spirit', and 36:26-27, which distinguishes 'a new spirit' from 'my rûaḥ'), and the compass side of the measured precinct (42:16-20, where 'sides' is required by the measurements). The entry is inferred, not direct, because transliteration is a decision to leave a recognized ambiguity unresolved; the commentary at each site sets out the readings. With Ezekiel, a Latter Prophet now applies the same practice as the two Kings overlays. That meets the condition the Kings overlays set for promoting the ruach transliteration to one central entry, and the wave-E2 editor report recommends it. **Ratification note (2026-11-01).** The founder ratified this entry at the wave-E2 sign-off, together with the Reviewer's flag on 11:19: the gift clause is narrowed so that a 'new spirit' given to the people is rendered 'spirit' (11:19; later 18:31; 36:26a), and 'ruach' is kept where rûaḥ moves the prophet or is YHWH's own rûaḥ given (37:5-6, 14; 36:27).

entries.lemma: personal names, toponyms and divine names in Ezekiel
entries.standardEnglish: ASV English forms (Israel, Judah, Jerusalem, Jaazaniah, Shaphan, Azzur, Pelatiah, Benaiah, Tammuz, Tel-abib, Chaldea, Chebar, Zadok, Levi)
entries.wohChoice: English forms for personal names and toponyms, as in the signed-off chapters of this book (Ezekiel, Judah, Joseph, Ephraim, David, Jacob, Israel): Israel, Judah, Jerusalem, Jaazaniah son of Shaphan (8:11), Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah (11:1, 13), Tammuz (8:14, the Hebrew article not rendered), Tel-abib (3:15), Zadok (40:46; 43:19; 44:15), Levi, Levites. Hebrew forms only where a central entry rules: Kebar (nehar-kevar) and Kasdim (eretz-kasdim), together with the corpus divine-name forms YHWH, Lord YHWH and Elohim.
entries.rationale: The ezekiel-woh chapters signed off in 2026-05 use English forms for names (37:16 'For Judah ... For Joseph — the stick of Ephraim'; 37:24-25 'David', 'Jacob'; 'Israel' throughout) and Hebrew forms only where a central entry decides otherwise (1:1, 3 'Kebar'; 1:3 'the land of the Kasdim'). The Kings overlays transliterate names under founder decision A (Yisra'el, Yehudah, Tzadoq), so the corpus now has two practices. This entry records Ezekiel's so that the founder can decide whether to align the books. Within one book a single practice must hold: introducing 'Yisra'el' or 'Tzadoq' into this wave would make it inconsistent with the three signed-off chapters, which are not to be retro-edited. Two forms need a note. The divine name hattammûz has the article, as habbaʿal does in Kings, and English convention, like the ASV and NRSV, drops it; the Mesopotamian deity is Dumuzi, under the central dumuzi-tammuz-adonis-dying-and-rising-vegetation-god-cross-corpus for the Akkadian sources. tēl ʾāḇîḇ is usually explained from Akkadian til abūbi 'mound of the flood' (Zimmerli; Block); the ASV form 'Tel-abib' is kept, distinct from the modern city name, which was taken from this verse in 1902.

entries.lemma: Ketiv ('what is written', the consonantal text) and Qere ('what is read', the Masoretic reading tradition)
entries.literal: the written consonants vs the vocalized reading
entries.standardEnglish: ASV and the major English versions translate the Qere, with occasional exceptions (ASV follows the Ketiv at Ezek 3:15)
entries.wohChoice: Translate the Qere and record the Ketiv in commentary at every site. Wave E2 (48 readings in 24 verses): 3:15 (K wʾšr 'and which' / Q wāʾēšēḇ 'and I sat', the only sense-changing pair; ASV follows the Ketiv); 8:6 (K mhm / Q mâ hēm, word division); 40:6, 9, 15, 21 (3), 22 (4), 24 (2), 25, 26 (3), 29 (4), 31 (2), 33 (4), 34 (3), 36 (3), 37 (3) (defective spelling -w of the plural suffix -āyw on maʿălôṯ 'steps', tāʾ 'guardroom', ʾayil 'post', ʾêlām 'vestibule', ḥallôn 'window', timōrâ 'palm-tree', ʿōlâ/maʿăleh 'ascent'; 40:15 K hyʾtwn / Q hāʾîṯôn 'the entrance'); 42:9 (K wmtḥth lškwt / Q ûmittaḥaṯ hallǝšāḵôṯ, word division and article; K hmbwʾ / Q hammēḇîʾ 'the entry'); 42:14 (K ylbšw / Q wəlāḇəšû); 42:16 (K ʾmwt 'cubits' / Q mēʾôṯ 'hundreds'); 43:11 (K ṣwrty / Q ṣûrōṯāyw; K twrtw / Q tôrōṯāyw); 43:16 (K hʾrʾyl / Q hāʾărîʾêl); 43:26 (K ydw / Q yāḏāyw); 44:5 (K twrtw / Q tôrōṯāyw); 44:24 (K lšpṭ / Q ləmišpāṭ; K wšpṭhw / Q yišpəṭûhû).
entries.rationale: The Leningrad Codex marks each Ketiv/Qere pair, and the source edition prints the Ketiv consonants followed by the vocalized Qere in brackets. The Masoretic tradition reads the Qere, and English translation, including the ASV baseline, follows it in all but a few cases (Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed., 2012). This is the corpus baseline in genesis-woh, exodus-woh and the Kings overlays (ketiv-qere-qere-translated-kings), and this entry makes it explicit for Ezekiel so that later waves can extend the list. Most of the wave-E2 pairs are orthographic: the 37 readings in ch. 40 and several in chs. 43-44 spell the third-person plural suffix -āyw with a bare waw (-w), an older defective spelling that does not affect the sense. Two pairs are differences of word division (8:6; 42:9a). Only 3:15 changes the meaning ('and I sat' vs 'and which / to where'); the ASV follows the Ketiv there ('and to where they dwelt'), and this translation, like most modern versions, follows the Qere. At 42:16 the Ketiv 'cubits' cannot be construed with qānîm 'reeds', and the Qere 'hundreds' is supported by vv 17-19. Where the Qere stands at verse end (40:26, 31, 34, 37; 43:26) the source places the sof pasuq inside the bracket; the Hebrew text is kept as delivered. The translator's draft counted 46 readings in 25 verses; a script over the source finds 48 readings in 24 verses, the figure used here.

entries.translit: gôyim hammôrəḏîm ; bārûḵ ; ʾēš ; ʾappām ; hôṣîʾ ; qānîm ; bəḇōʾî ; wayyāp̄ērû ; pisqa / setumah ...
entries.lemma: the Masoretic consonants, vocalization, word division and paragraph marks where the ancient versions (LXX, Peshitta, Vulgate, Theodotion) or modern emendations read otherwise
entries.standardEnglish: the ASV follows the MT at most of these sites; NRSV adopts the versional reading at 3:12, 8:2, 11:15, 40:44, 42:4, 42:10, 42:16 and 43:3
entries.wohChoice: Translate the MT and give the versional or conjectural reading in commentary. Wave E2 sites: 2:3 'to nations that are rebelling' (LXX lacks 'nations'); 2:7 'for they are rebellious' (some witnesses 'a rebellious house'); 3:12 'Blessed be the glory of YHWH' (emendation bərûm 'as ... rose'); 8:2 'like the appearance of fire' (LXX 'of a man'); 8:16 the anomalous mištaḥăwîṯem rendered as the participle; 8:17 'to their nose' (tiqqûn sōp̄ərîm, 'to my nose'); 11:3 statement (LXX question); 11:7 MT hôṣîʾ rendered impersonally (versions 'I will bring out'); 11:15 'the men of your kindred' (LXX 'your exile') and the imperative 'Keep far'; 11:19 'one heart' (LXX 'another') and 'within you' (versions 'within them'); 11:21 no emendation of wəʾel-lēḇ; 40:2 'on it' (LXX 'opposite'); 40:6 the repeated threshold; 40:8 the verse that duplicates 40:9a; 40:14 the obscure 'sixty cubits'; 40:30 (absent in LXX); 40:37 'its posts' (LXX 'vestibules'); 40:44 'chambers for the singers ... the east gate' (LXX 'two chambers ... the south gate'); 40:48-49 (LXX 'fourteen cubits', 'twelve', 'ten steps'); 42:4 'one cubit' (LXX 'a hundred'); 42:10 'east' (LXX 'south'); 42:12 the hapax hăḡînâ translated ('corresponding'), not omitted; 42:16 'reeds' (LXX 'cubits'); 43:3 'when I came' (versions 'he came'); 43:7 bāmôṯām 'their high places' (others 'at their death'); 43:11 the repeated 'all its forms'; 44:3 the anomalous pointing of leʾĕḵôl reproduced; 44:7 'they broke' (versions 'you broke'); 44:19 the repeated 'into the outer court'; 44:28 the positive 'for an inheritance' (Vulgate negative). Words are supplied only where the English needs them to construe the MT (8:3 'court'; 43:7 'this is'; 44:8 'them'), not where it construes without them (43:16-17: no 'cubits'). Masoretic paragraph marks stay in the Hebrew text, including the mid-verse pisqa at 3:16 and setumah at 43:27; the English is not broken there, and the commentary records them.
entries.rationale: The Wheel of Heaven Translation translates the Masoretic Text and records ancient-version and conjectural readings in the apparatus. This is the baseline of genesis-woh, exodus-woh and the Kings overlays (mt-baseline-at-versional-cruxes-and-versification-kings). Ezekiel has one of the most difficult Hebrew texts in the Bible, and its Old Greek is often shorter; Zimmerli (Ezekiel 1-2, Hermeneia, 1979-1983) and the NRSV adopt many versional readings, whereas the ASV, Greenberg (AB 22, 22A) and Block (NICOT) give more weight to the MT. At every wave-E2 site listed the MT gives a construable sense, even if a difficult one (40:14; 42:12; 44:3), or a sense that a versional reading would smooth (8:2; 42:16; 44:28). Emending would be a textual-critical decision beyond the remit of a translation that commits to the MT, so the alternatives are given in commentary. In particular, the conjecture bərûm at 3:12 is attractive and widely adopted, but bārûḵ is what the MT and the liturgical tradition (the Qedushah) read, and it can be construed as a cry heard in the noise. The paragraph marks are part of the Masoretic text, and the mid-verse marks at 3:16 and 43:27 are kept in the Hebrew field and explained in commentary rather than imposed on the English. Supplying words only where the English cannot construe without them is the minimum needed to keep the line a translation and not a paraphrase.

entries.literal: the sound of a great quaking
entries.standardEnglish: a voice of a great rushing (KJV, ASV); the sound of loud rumbling (NRSV)
entries.wohChoice: 'the sound of a great rumbling' (3:12, 13). At 37:7 (signed off) the same noun is 'a rattling', of bones coming together; both renderings lie within the lexical field and are chosen by context.
entries.rationale: raʿaš is the noun of rāʿaš 'quake, shake' (BDB; HALOT): it names the earthquake (1 Kgs 19:11-12; Amos 1:1; Zech 14:5), the rumble or rattle of chariot wheels (Nah 3:2 qôl raʿaš ʾôp̄ān 'the sound of the rumbling of the wheel'; Jer 47:3), and the rattling of a javelin (Job 41:21 [ET 41:29]). In Ezek 3:13 the noise is explicitly that of the living creatures' wings and of the wheels (ʾôp̄annîm), the same collocation as Nahum. 'Rumbling' (NRSV) gives that lexical sense. The KJV/ASV 'rushing' renders the impression of rapid motion, which the root does not express. The change touches a verse quoted in the Raëlian canon (KJV 'a voice of a great rushing'; French 'grande rumeur'); the reception reading is recorded in a labelled note and does not depend on the English word. The entry is direct because the rendering follows the lexica and current versions.

entries.literal: a chamber opening off a passage
entries.standardEnglish: little chamber (KJV); lodge (ASV); side room (RSV); recess (NRSV)
entries.wohChoice: 'guardroom(s)' for the three chambers on each side of the passage of each gate (40:7, 10, 12-13, 16, 21, 29, 33, 36)
entries.rationale: Outside Ezek 40 the noun occurs only at 1 Kgs 14:28 // 2 Chr 12:11, tāʾ hārāṣîm, the guardroom of the royal runners where the bronze shields were kept, which is the basis of the lexica's gloss (BDB 'chamber (guard-chamber)'; HALOT 'guardroom'). In Ezekiel's gate-buildings the tāʾîm are six chambers, three on each side of the passage (40:10), each six cubits square (40:7, 12). This plan matches the six-chamber city gates excavated at Megiddo, Hazor and Gezer (Yadin, IEJ 8, 1958), a comparison standard in the commentaries (Zimmerli, Ezekiel 2; Block, Ezekiel 25-48). The ASV 'lodge' now suggests a separate building, and 'recess' or 'side room' leave the function unstated; 'guardroom' gives the attested function. The decision is lexical and architectural and carries no interpretive content.

entries.lemma: ʾêlām, a by-form of ʾûlām 'porch, vestibule'
entries.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine (plural forms ʾêlammôṯ, and ʾêlammāyw with suffix)
entries.wohChoice: 'vestibule' / 'vestibules' (40:16, 21-22, 24-26, 29-31, 33-34, 36), keeping the central 'porch' for the spelling ʾûlām (40:7-9, 15, 39-40, 48-49; 44:3)
entries.rationale: The spelling ʾêlām / ʾēlām occurs only in Ezek 40. The lexica treat it as a by-form of ʾûlām 'porch' (BDB places it with ʾûlām; HALOT), and most interpreters take the ʾêlām of each gate as its vestibule, the element also called ʾûlām haššaʿar 'the porch of the gate' in 40:7-9, 15 and 39-40 (Zimmerli; Block). The KJV/ASV 'arches' has no lexical support. Two considerations shape the choice. First, the central Temple-plan entry (ulam-hekhal-devir-temple-three-room-plan-cross-corpus) rules ʾûlām 'porch'. Rendering ʾêlām 'porch' as well would hide the separate spelling, so 'vestibule' (NRSV) gives the same architectural sense while keeping the Hebrew difference visible. Second, the plural forms are not fully explained: the Qere ʾêlammāyw gives a gate several 'vestibules', and 40:30 ('vestibules all around, twenty-five cubits long and five cubits wide', absent in the LXX) does not fit the gate porch of 40:9. Some scholars therefore propose other senses ('jambs', 'pilasters', 'porticoes'). The entry is inferred, not direct: the lexical identification is the majority view, but its application to every plural form is a reasoned choice in a disputed passage.

entries.lemma: ʾayil II 'pilaster, projecting pier' (homonym of ʾayil 'ram' and ʾayil 'terebinth')
entries.standardEnglish: post(s) (KJV, ASV); jamb(s) or pilaster(s) (modern versions)
entries.wohChoice: 'post(s)' for the architectural ʾayil (40:9-10, 14, 16, 21, 24, 26, 29, 31, 33-34, 36-38, 48-49), kept apart from ʿammûḏ 'pillar' (40:49; 42:6) and from ʾayil 'ram' (43:23, 25)
entries.rationale: In Ezek 40-41 ʾayil is a projecting wall-pier or pilaster at the gate passage and at the porches (40:9 'its posts, two cubits'; 40:48 'the post of the porch, five cubits'), and it carries the carved palm ornaments (40:16, 26, 31). BDB lists it as ʾayil II 'pilaster, projecting pillar' and HALOT as 'pilaster, jamb'; it also occurs at 1 Kgs 6:31. The ASV 'post' is plain English and does not prejudge whether the element is an engaged pier or a jamb. The text distinguishes the freestanding ʿammûḏ 'pillar' (40:49), so a different English word is needed for each. The homonym ʾayil 'ram' appears in the altar rite (43:23, 25) and is rendered 'ram' there. The entry records the distinction so that readers can follow the three words.

entries.literal: bosom / back, raised surface / border, rim / enclosure, stage / span (half a cubit)
entries.standardEnglish: ASV: bottom / base / border / ledge / span (KJV 'settle' for ʿăzārâ, 'higher place' for gab); NRSV: base / height / rim / ledge / span
entries.wohChoice: the ASV terms: ḥêq 'bottom' (43:13-14, 17), gab 'base' (43:13), gəḇûl 'border' (43:13, 17, 20), ʿăzārâ 'ledge' (43:14, 17, 20), zereṯ 'span' (43:13)
entries.rationale: Ezek 43:13-17 describes a stepped altar: a base set in a trench (ḥêq, literally 'bosom'), a lower and an upper stage (ʿăzārâ, 'lower/smaller' and 'greater'), each set back by a cubit, and the hearth with its four horns (see harel-ariel-altar-hearth-ezekiel-43). ʿăzārâ elsewhere means a court or enclosure (2 Chr 4:9; 6:13), and here it is the ledge of each stage; gəḇûl is a rim or kerb; zereṯ is the span, half a cubit (Ex 28:16). gab 'back, raised surface' is the hardest term: the ASV 'base' takes it as a summary of the foundation just described, and NRSV 'height' takes it of the altar's elevation. The ASV is kept and the alternative recorded. The ASV terms are descriptive and neutral and fit the measurements. Albright's comparison of the stepped form to the Mesopotamian ziggurat (Archaeology and the Religion of Israel, 1942) is recorded in commentary and not built into the line.

entries.literal: harʾēl: vocalized as if 'mountain of El'; ʾărîʾēl: altar hearth
entries.standardEnglish: upper altar (43:15a) / altar hearth (43:15b, 16) (ASV); altar hearth throughout (NRSV)
entries.rationale: The topmost block of the altar, twelve by twelve and bearing the four horns, is named three times in two verses with three spellings: harʾēl (43:15a), ʾăriʾêl (43:15b) and the Ketiv hʾrʾyl / Qere hāʾărîʾêl (43:16). ʾărîʾēl is attested as a cult object in the Mesha inscription (line 12) and as a name for Jerusalem in Isa 29:1-2 ('she shall be to me as an ʾărîʾēl'), and it is generally taken as 'altar hearth' (BDB; HALOT). harʾēl is usually explained as a variant spelling or as a Masoretic reinterpretation of the same word as 'mountain of El'; Albright (1942) compared Akkadian arallû. The ASV gives two different terms ('upper altar' / 'altar hearth') for what the measurements show to be one element, and 'upper altar' has no lexical basis. The line uses 'altar hearth' for all three spellings, as NRSV does, and the commentary records harʾēl and its possible reading. The entry is inferred because it takes two Masoretic vocalizations as one word.

entries.source: אַמָּה / טֹפַח / זֶרֶת / קָנֶה (קְנֵה הַמִּדָּה) / פְּתִיל
entries.translit: ʾammâ / ṭōp̄aḥ / zereṯ / qāneh (qənēh hammiddâ) / pəṯîl
entries.lemma: units and instruments of measurement in Ezek 40-48
entries.standardEnglish: cubit / handbreadth / span / reed / line (ASV); NRSV the same units, sometimes with metric notes
entries.wohChoice: the ancient units in the line ('cubit', 'handbreadth', 'span', 'reed'), numbers written out in words, no metric conversions in the line; the measuring instruments 'the measuring reed' and 'a cord of flax' (40:3). The long cubit, ʾammâ wāṭōp̄aḥ 'a cubit and a handbreadth' (40:5; 43:13), is rendered literally, and its value (about 52 cm, against about 45 cm for the common cubit; the reed about 3.1 m) is given in commentary.
entries.rationale: Ezekiel's temple vision is a sequence of measurements, and its units are part of what the text says. Converting them in the line would add precision the Hebrew does not have (the length of the cubit varied, and Ezekiel defines his own long cubit) and would date the translation. The ASV and the major versions keep the ancient units, and the corpus does the same (1 Kgs 6-7, 'cubits'). Ezekiel's 'cubit and a handbreadth' (seven handbreadths instead of six) matches the 'cubits of the old measure' of 2 Chr 3:3, the royal cubit attested in Egypt and Mesopotamia. The approximate values are given once in commentary (40:5) for readers who want them. Numbers are written in words, as in the ASV. Where the Hebrew gives a number without a unit (43:16-17) no unit is supplied (see mt-baseline-at-versional-cruxes-ezekiel).

entries.lemma: tabnîṯ 'pattern, form, model' (bnh 'build'); toḵnîṯ 'measurement, proportion' (tkn 'measure, regulate'); təḵûnâ 'arrangement, fixed place' (tkn)
entries.wohChoice: tabnîṯ 'pattern' (8:3 'the pattern of a hand'; 8:10 'every pattern of creeping thing', as 10:8 'the pattern of a human hand'); toḵnîṯ 'plan' (43:10 'let them measure the plan'); təḵûnâ 'arrangement' (43:11)
entries.rationale: Three related nouns need three English words. tabnîṯ, from bnh 'build', is the pattern or model of something (Ex 25:9, 40, the tabernacle 'pattern'; 2 Kgs 16:10; 1 Chr 28:11-19), and in Ezekiel's visions it describes what looks like a hand or a creature (8:3, 10; 10:8). The signed-off 10:8 renders it 'pattern', and this wave follows that rendering in place of the ASV 'form'. toḵnîṯ, from tkn 'measure, weigh, regulate', is a measured proportion or plan (BDB; HALOT; elsewhere only at 28:12). Rendering it 'pattern' as the ASV does at 43:10 would give two different lexemes the same English word, so 'plan' is used. təḵûnâ (43:11, same root) is the arrangement or layout of the house (ASV 'fashion'), rendered 'arrangement'. The distinctions are lexical and carry no interpretive content.

entries.standardEnglish: thou hast delivered thy soul (KJV, ASV); you will have saved your life (NRSV, NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'life' where nep̄eš is the person's own life that is saved or lost (3:19, 21 'you have delivered your life'), following the Kings practice (nefesh-scope-and-spelling-kings); the transliteration 'nefesh' is reserved for passages that name the nep̄eš as the life-component that departs or returns
entries.rationale: nep̄eš covers the throat, the breath of life, the living person and the self (BDB; HALOT; Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, 1974). In the watchman oracle the contrast is between the wicked man who 'shall die in his iniquity' and the watchman who, by warning him, escapes the bloodguilt of v 18 ('his blood I will require from your hand'). What the watchman saves is his own life, as the parallel at 33:5, 9 and the idiom elsewhere show (Gen 19:17; 1 Sam 19:11). The ASV 'soul' suggests the later concept of an immortal soul, which the passage does not address. The Kings overlays render the same idiomatic uses 'life' or a reflexive, and NRSV and NJPS have 'life' here. The entry brings Ezekiel into line with that practice.

entries.literal: the officials of the people / the prince
entries.standardEnglish: princes of the people (ASV 11:1); the prince (ASV 44:3); officials of the people (NRSV 11:1)
entries.wohChoice: śārîm 'officials' (11:1 'officials of the people'); nāśîʾ 'prince' (44:3, as 37:25 'David my servant shall be their prince')
entries.rationale: Ezekiel gives the title nāśîʾ to the future Davidic ruler (34:24; 37:25) and to the ruler of the restored community, whose rights and duties occupy chs. 44-48 (44:3; 45:7-17, 22; 46:2-18). Readers need to be able to follow that term. The ASV uses 'princes' also for śārîm at 11:1, the court officials of Jerusalem, which would make two different offices look like one. śar is the general word for an official, officer or commander (BDB; HALOT), and NRSV has 'officials of the people' at 11:1. Keeping 'prince' for nāśîʾ follows the signed-off 37:25 and the central nasi-elohim-honorific ('a prince of Elohim', Gen 23:6). The decision is lexical.

entries.source: כִּי־קֹדֶשׁ הֵנָּה / לִשְׁכוֹת הַקֹּדֶשׁ / וְלֹא־יְקַדְּשׁוּ אֶת־הָעָם בְּבִגְדֵיהֶם
entries.translit: kî-qōḏeš hēnnâ / liškôṯ haqqōḏeš / wəlōʾ-yəqaddəšû ʾeṯ-hāʿām bəḇiḡḏêhem
entries.lemma: qōḏeš 'holiness, holy thing'; qiddēš 'make holy, sanctify'
entries.literal: for they are holiness / the chambers of holiness / and they shall not make the people holy with their garments
entries.standardEnglish: for they are holy; the holy chambers; that they sanctify not the people with their garments (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: 'holy' / 'the holy chambers' (42:13-14); 'so that they do not sanctify the people with their garments' (44:19)
entries.rationale: qōḏeš is the ordinary Hebrew noun for holiness, used here as a predicate of the priestly vestments (42:14) and of the chambers where the most holy offerings are eaten (42:13). The rule that the vestments must be left in the holy chambers rests on the Priestly idea that holiness passes by contact (Lev 6:11, 20 [ET 6:18, 27]; Ezek 44:19; 46:20; Hag 2:12; Milgrom, Leviticus 1-16, AB 3, 1991, on contagious holiness). The renderings are those of every major version. The entry exists because 42:14 is quoted in the Raëlian canon, which proposes 'healthful' (French sains) for 'holy' (saints). That wordplay works only in French and has no counterpart in the Hebrew, which uses qōḏeš and not a word of the health field (šālôm, rp'). The line renders qōḏeš lexically, and the canon's reading is recorded in a labelled reception note.

entries.partOfSpeech: noun phrase (construct); passive participle with adverbial nouns
entries.literal: a roll of a document / written face and back
entries.standardEnglish: a roll of a book ... written within and without (ASV, KJV); a written scroll ... on the front and on the back (NRSV)
entries.wohChoice: 'a scroll of a book' (2:9; 'this scroll', 3:1-3) and 'written on the front and on the back' (2:10)
entries.rationale: məḡillat-sēp̄er is a scroll, a rolled document (Jer 36:2, 4; Ps 40:8 [ET 40:7]). 'Scroll' is today's English for the ASV 'roll' with the same sense. pānîm and ʾāḥôr are 'face' and 'back' (BDB), so the scroll is written on both sides. The KJV/ASV 'within and without' expresses the same thing in older English, but a modern reader may take it as the inside and outside of a container. The literal rendering is the one NRSV adopts. Scrolls were normally written on one side only, and commentators remark on the detail (Greenberg, AB 22, takes it to mean the scroll was full); Rev 5:1 ('written within and on the back') echoes the verse. The verses are quoted in the Raëlian canon, whose reading is recorded in a labelled reception note; the rendering is lexical.
